Q: View query results from a PL/SQL block without PUT_LINE, RETURN_RESULTS, or CREATE? A:

The issue is that SELECT QTest(v_ID) FROM DUAL returns the ref cursor as one opaque column, not an expanded rowset which only works when a client explicitly binds a REF CURSOR OUT param, not from a plain SELECT.

Since you can't create objects, skip ref cursors entirely and use dbms_xmlgen + XMLTABLE to turn your dynamic SQL into XML, then shred it back into a normal rowset in the same statement. If you are using oracle-12.1, just build the SQL string directly inside getxmltype() instead

Q: How to launch Windows' RegEdit with certain path? A:

Just by using a (admin) Command Prompt batch.
(This applies on All Windows versions. At least from Vista and over.)

This is the best answer overall, as it's quick, simple and there's no need to install any program.
By Byron Persino, improved by Matt Miller. (Many thanks to both of them!)

Make a .bat file, eg. 'GoToRegEditPath.bat' , write the following code inside and save it:

@echo off
set /p regPath="Open regedit at path: " 
REG ADD HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Applets\Regedit /v LastKey /t REG_SZ /d "%regPath%" /f
START regedit

Maybe this .bat use must "Run as Administrator"
To use it, Just run it and paste (R-Click) in it the copied RegEdit Path.

Tip: if R-click does not work inside command prompt:
R-click on title bar > Properties > check both under "Edit Options"

An improved version of the above batch will support multiple instances of regedit.exe:

Open the Windows Registry Editor (regedit.exe) to a new proccess on specific HKEY.

@echo off
echo. Open a new process of Windows Registry Editor on specific HKEY.&echo.
echo. Paste here the HKEY:
set /p "HKEY=Paste here the HKEY:" >nul
reg add "HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Applets\Regedit" /v LastKey /t REG_SZ /d "%HKEY%" /f
start "" "%SystemRoot%\regedit.exe" -m

If you start the regedit.exe with -m switch will be open in separate process. ;)

Q: How to use AI as programmer A:

AI should enhance your programming skills, not replace your thinking.

Here are a few practices that have worked well for me:

• Use ChatGPT or Claude to understand concepts instead of copying code blindly.

• Ask AI to explain why a solution works before implementing it.

• Break complex problems into smaller tasks and verify every output.

• Read the official documentation after getting an AI-generated answer.

• Debug errors yourself first, then use AI to identify what you might have missed.

• Build small projects without AI occasionally to strengthen problem-solving skills.

AI is an excellent productivity assistant, but long-term growth still depends on understanding algorithms, system design, debugging, and writing maintainable code. Developers who combine AI with strong fundamentals will benefit the most.
